text: And one last mistake, the email box that appears with nothing in it. Back to our contact form. When the user ticks Email me a reply, an email box should appear. The double ampersand from lesson ten shows the box only when wantsReply is true. This piece lives in ContactForm.jsx. Line one opens curly braces with wantsReply, the double ampersand, and a parenthesis. Inside, there's a label that says Email and an input with value equals email in curly braces. Its onChange takes e.target.value and passes it to setEmail. Then the label closes, and the parenthesis and the curly brace close on line six. The email is not needed until the box is ticked, so the developer gives its state no starting value. It's just one line, line eight of the same file. Email and setEmail from useState with empty parentheses. The note calls it wrong because it's undefined until the first key. The user ticks Email me a reply, and an empty email box appears. The user types A, and the warning appears. Figure twenty-five has the whole contact form on screen. The heading Contact Us, the name Anna, the topic Payment, and a message counter at zero out of two hundred. Email me a reply is ticked, and the new email box holds the letter A right above the Send button. And in the console, it's the same red message as before. A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled, likely because the value changed from undefined to a defined value. [sighs] Same warning, same link to React.dev. The steps are the same as for the city box, and the fix is one empty string. Back on line eight, email and setEmail now come from useState with an empty string, two quotes with nothing between them. That's a real string from the first render. After a reload, typing into the email box gives no warning. And finally, send clears the whole form. Now the send handler empties the email too. Every state goes back to its start, and no line of our code touches a box. Down at line sixteen of ContactForm.jsx, the function handleSend receives the event, e. Line seventeen calls e.preventDefault, so the page does not reload. Line eighteen logs the word "Sent," followed by name, topic, message, wantsReply, and email. Then the clearing starts. SetName with an empty string, setTopic back to Delivery, setMessage with an empty string, setWantsReply to false, and on line twenty-three, setEmail with an empty string. Never undefined, as the note says. Notice that the email is cleared with an empty string. Clearing a box with undefined or null would make it switch the other way, from controlled to uncontrolled. So we clear with the same kind of value we started with. So principle five: the starting value. A controlled box starts with an empty string. The state behind value must hold a string from the first render, so the state of an empty box starts as an empty string, never as nothing. A useState call with no starting value gives undefined. An undefined value is the same as no value at all, so the box starts uncontrolled. On the first key, state becomes a string, the box becomes controlled, and React warns because a box cannot switch over its life. An empty string makes the box controlled from the first render. And clear it with an empty string too. So do this: email and setEmail from useState with an empty string, controlled from the first render. And don't do this: email and setEmail from useState with nothing at all. That's undefined first, a string later, so React warns.
